verdicts.trueWording: The first AI model made for fiction, just for storytellers like you.
verdicts.note: Live fetch 200. Exact string 'The first AI model made for fiction' present (with <em> on 'fiction'); hero variant 'The first AI made for fiction, designed for authors'; <title> 'the only AI model made for fiction'. 'rather than general assistance' limb supported by the panel pair 'Basic AI writes boring emails.' / 'Muse is just for fiction' and the JSON-LD featureList 'Better at storytelling than general models like ChatGPT'.

Quote is verbatim as an <h1> comparison heading, paired with 'Muse writes unique prose every single time'. Core is supported: the marketing does name cliché as a defect of 'Basic AI' (foil labelled ChatGPT). But the page presents three parallel defect headings, so singling cliché out as *the* characteristic defect is not what the page says. 'general-purpose models' is a fair reading of 'Basic AI'.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that cliché is *the* characteristic defect — the page gives three co-equal 'Basic AI' defect headings (boring emails, clichés, happy endings), not one

verdicts.note: Verbatim as a feature pill in the list under 'Peerless prose. Muse has a deep understanding of writing craft and avoids the pitfalls of other models.', alongside 'Show, Don't Tell', 'Dynamic Pacing', 'Readability Optimization', etc. Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Two separate annotations: 'too much exposition!' then 'way too telly …'
verdicts.note: Both annotations are on the page, in that order, on the ChatGPT foil sample ('In the year 2150, Earth had undergone a remarkable transformation...'), followed by a third, 'try adding more detail?'. They sit in DIFFERENT RichTextContainer divs (framer-bcfl9u and framer-r643vh, different rotations), so the claimed run 'too much exposition! way too telly' is not one contiguous verbatim string — hence SUBSTANCE, not VERBATIM. Every limb of the claim is supported.

Both lines sit inside ONE annotation div (framer-icgfed) as two

children, i.e. a single handwritten bubble broken over two lines — contiguous verbatim text. It annotates the second ChatGPT foil sample ('Her thoughts raced as she reread the email...') in the 'Basic AI spews clichés.' comparison, alongside 'so many cliches', 'where is the tension?', 'is this a romance?'.

verdicts.trueWording: Muse ... avoids the pitfalls of other models
verdicts.note: Full sentence on page: 'Peerless prose. Muse has a deep understanding of writing craft and avoids the pitfalls of other models.' Quote verbatim; the 'craft' limb is carried by 'deep understanding of writing craft' in the same sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: it was like reading ChatGPT responses I had generated myself
verdicts.note: Verbatim, inside the parenthesis beginning 'Why do I think this?' as located: 'As soon as I read the first pages of these fake books, it was like reading ChatGPT responses I had generated myself.)' Context is the books credited to her on Amazon/Goodreads that she did not write.

verdicts.trueWording: Please provide us with any trademark registration numbers that relate to your claim.
verdicts.note: Verbatim in 'Update (afternoon of Aug. 7)': she filed a report with Amazon that the books used her name without consent; 'Amazon's response: "Please provide us with any trademark registration numbers that relate to your claim."' She adds that when she said she had no trademark, Amazon closed the case.

verdicts.trueWording: 23 percent of writers reported using generative AI as part of their writing process.
verdicts.note: Verbatim under 'Survey Results' > 'Use of Generative AI Technologies'. Page is dated May 15, 2023 (datePublished 2023-05-15) and states 'More than 1,700 authors from diverse backgrounds took part.' Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Only around 7 percent of writers who employ generative AI said they use it to generate the text of their work.
verdicts.note: Verbatim, closing the same paragraph as the 47/29/14/26 percent breakdown, in 'Use of Generative AI Technologies'. Scoping ('of the writers who use generative AI') matches the page exactly.

verdicts.trueWording: 89 percent reported that less than 10 percent of their final work included generative AI output.
verdicts.note: Verbatim as the second clause of: 'Only 1.4 percent of the writers who said they use generative AI to generate the text of their work said that AI-generated text comprised 50 percent or more of their work; 89 percent reported that...'. The claim's scoping to text-generating users is the sentence's own subject set.

verdicts.trueWording: 91 percent of authors surveyed believe readers should know when AI has created all or even portions of a work.
verdicts.note: Verbatim under the section heading 'Concerns About Authenticity, Market Dilution', exactly as cited. Claim's 'all or part of a work' tracks the page's 'all or even portions of a work'.

verdicts.trueWording: the number of spam submissions resulting in bans has hit 38% this month
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the paragraph beginning 'What I can say'. Post byline reads 'On 02/15/2023', and the body says 'This is being published on the 15th of February', so 'this month' = February 2023. Page's word 'spam' is dropped by the claim but names the same set (bans are for spam submissions).

verdicts.trueWording: There are some very obvious patterns and I have no intention of helping those people become less likely to be caught.
verdicts.note: Verbatim, in the paragraph beginning 'I'm not going to detail how I know these stories are "AI" spam or outline any of the data I have collected from these submissions.' Both limbs — declining to publish the patterns, and refusing to help senders evade detection — are on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: they are prone to false negatives and positives
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the paragraph beginning 'Yes, there are tools out there for detecting plagiarized and machine-written text, but they are prone to false negatives and positives.' Both false negatives and false positives named.
